evidence: Fields `private readonly users = new Map<string, User>()`, `projects`, `tasks` and the counters `nextUserId`/`nextProjectId`/`nextTaskId` store data in memory and generate IDs. This is repository/persistence work and belongs to infrastructure.
`this.tasks.set(task.id, task)` in createTask, `this.users.set` in createUser and `this.projects.set` in createProject write to storage directly. This is persistence and belongs to infrastructure.
`[...this.tasks.values()].filter(...)` in listProjectTasks runs a storage query inside the service. This is a repository concern and belongs to infrastructure.
markTaskDone: `if (task.status === "done") throw new DomainError("Task is already done", 409)` is a task state-transition rule. It belongs to the domain.
requireText, requireStatus and validateDueDate check entity validity (required title/description, allowed statuses, valid due date). These rules belong to the domain.
`new DomainError("User not found", 404)` / `new DomainError(..., 409)` put HTTP status codes in the application service. That is a transport concern and belongs to infrastructure/presentation.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: TaskManagementService is in the application layer, so its job should be orchestrating use cases. The file does more than that. First, it stores and looks up data itself: it keeps users, projects and tasks in private Maps, generates sequential IDs, and does lookups and filtering in getUser, getProject, getTask and listProjectTasks. That is repository work, which belongs to the infrastructure layer. It should sit behind a port, not be built into the service. Second, it holds domain rules for the entities. requireText, requireStatus and validateDueDate check what makes a valid entity. The rule in markTaskDone that a task already done cannot be marked done again is a task state-transition rule. Building entities directly (trimming values, defaulting status to "todo") is also entity logic. All of this belongs in the domain layer, but here it is hard-coded in the application service. Third, it chooses HTTP status codes (404, 409) when it throws DomainError, which ties use-case logic to transport. Taken together, the file carries responsibilities from several layer kinds, so it fails the rule.

violations.message: TaskManagementService stores data itself: it keeps users, projects and tasks in Maps (the users, projects and tasks fields), generates IDs with the nextUserId, nextProjectId and nextTaskId counters, and queries storage in getUser, getProject, getTask and listProjectTasks. This is repository/persistence work that belongs to infrastructure behind a port.

Domain rules are built into the application service. markTaskDone enforces the 'already done' state-transition rule, and requireText, requireStatus and validateDueDate enforce entity validity. These belong to the domain layer (Task/User/Project entities).

HTTP status codes (404 in getUser, getProject and getTask; 409 in markTaskDone) are hard-coded in the DomainErrors the service throws. That ties the service to a transport concern which belongs to infrastructure/presentation.
